conversation.content: Hey, I've been reading about adversarial machine learning for my thesis and I'm a bit confused about the difference between white-box and black-box attacks. Can you break that down for me?

conversation.label: benign
conversation.content: Sure, happy to help with your thesis! In adversarial ML, the distinction comes down to how much information the attacker has about the target model. In a white-box attack, the adversary has full access to the model — including its architecture, weights, gradients, and training data. This lets them craft highly optimized adversarial examples using methods like FGSM (Fast Gradient Sign Method) or PGD (Projected Gradient Descent). In a black-box attack, the adversary can only query the model and observe outputs — they don't know the internals. They typically rely on transferability of adversarial examples or use surrogate models to approximate the target. Does that distinction make sense for your context?

conversation.label: benign
conversation.content: Yes, that helps a lot! My thesis is focused on image classifiers specifically. I keep seeing FGSM mentioned everywhere. Is it still considered relevant or is it kind of outdated at this point?

conversation.label: benign
conversation.content: FGSM is definitely still relevant, especially as a baseline and for understanding adversarial robustness fundamentals. It was introduced by Goodfellow et al. in 2014 and works by taking a single step in the direction of the gradient of the loss with respect to the input. It's computationally cheap and easy to implement, which is why it's widely used in papers as a quick sanity check. That said, it's considered a relatively weak attack compared to iterative methods like PGD or AutoAttack. Many defense papers that claim robustness against FGSM have later been shown to be vulnerable to stronger attacks — a phenomenon sometimes called 'gradient masking.' So for a rigorous thesis, you'd want to evaluate against stronger benchmarks too, but FGSM is a great starting point conceptually.

conversation.label: benign
conversation.content: That's really interesting about gradient masking. I've also seen the term 'obfuscated gradients' — are those the same thing?

conversation.label: benign
conversation.content: Great question — they're closely related but not exactly the same. 'Obfuscated gradients' is actually a more specific and formalized term introduced in a 2018 paper by Athalye et al. titled 'Obfuscated Gradients Give a False Sense of Security.' It describes three main failure modes that make gradient-based attacks ineffective against a defense, not because the defense is truly robust, but because the gradients become uninformative or vanishing. These include shattered gradients (non-differentiable operations), stochastic gradients (randomness in the forward pass), and exploding/vanishing gradients. Gradient masking is the broader, more colloquial term that encompasses these and similar phenomena. The Athalye paper was really influential because it broke many defenses that had been published at top venues, by using techniques like BPDA (Backward Pass Differentiable Approximation) to work around the obfuscation.

conversation.label: benign
conversation.content: Wow, I definitely need to read that paper. For my thesis, I'm planning to implement adversarial training as a defense. Is that still considered the gold standard?

conversation.label: benign
conversation.content: Adversarial training is widely considered the most empirically reliable defense we have right now, yes. The core idea is simple: you augment your training data with adversarial examples so the model learns to be robust to perturbations. Madry et al.'s PGD-based adversarial training from 2018 is often treated as the baseline gold standard. However, it does come with real trade-offs. There's a well-documented 'robustness-accuracy trade-off' — models trained adversarially typically have lower clean accuracy compared to standard models. Training is also computationally expensive since you're generating adversarial examples during each training iteration. More recent work like TRADES and MART try to better balance clean and robust accuracy. RobustBench is a great leaderboard to check for current state-of-the-art results. What dataset are you planning to work with — CIFAR-10, ImageNet, something else?

conversation.label: benign
conversation.content: I was thinking CIFAR-10 since it's manageable for my compute budget. I also heard about certified defenses — are those better than adversarial training in some cases?

conversation.label: benign
conversation.content: Certified defenses are a fascinating alternative! The key distinction is that adversarial training is empirical — it makes the model harder to fool in practice, but doesn't provide a formal guarantee. Certified defenses, on the other hand, provide provable robustness bounds, meaning they can mathematically guarantee that no perturbation within a certain epsilon ball can change the model's prediction. Methods like randomized smoothing (Cohen et al., 2019) and interval bound propagation (IBP) are popular certified approaches. The downside is that certified defenses typically have lower certified accuracy compared to the empirical robust accuracy of adversarially trained models, especially at larger epsilon values. They also tend to scale poorly to complex architectures. For CIFAR-10 at small epsilon values (like L-inf epsilon of 8/255), adversarial training generally outperforms certified methods in practice. But if your thesis angle is about formal guarantees, certified defenses are a really compelling research direction.

conversation.content: This is super helpful. One last question — when I write up my experiments, what metrics should I report to make the evaluation rigorous?

conversation.label: benign
conversation.content: Great thinking to plan this out upfront — evaluation rigor is actually a big issue in adversarial ML literature. Here's what you should generally report: First, clean accuracy — the model's accuracy on unperturbed test data, since it's important to show you haven't sacrificed too much standard performance. Second, robust accuracy under multiple attack strengths — don't just test one epsilon value; show a curve across a range to give a fuller picture. Third, make sure to evaluate against strong attacks like AutoAttack, which is an ensemble of parameter-free attacks and has become the community standard for reliable evaluation. Avoid evaluating only against FGSM, as that's considered insufficient. Fourth, if you're comparing defenses, report computational cost (training time, inference time). Fifth, consider reporting across multiple random seeds to show statistical reliability. Also, be transparent about your threat model — specify the perturbation norm (L-inf, L2, etc.) and epsilon value clearly. Reviewers and readers will take your work much more seriously if you follow these practices. Good luck with your thesis!
